title: The Astral Convergence
subtitle: The Planes Collide, and Reality Itself Hangs in the Balance
synopsis:
For eons the Astral Sea has been the silent highway between worlds — a vast silver void where the thoughts of gods drift like continents and the corpses of dead deities tumble through timeless space. It is not a place of conflict. It is a place of passage, of memory, of things that once were and things that might yet be. But something has changed. The boundaries between planes have begun to buckle. The Astral Sea churns with color-storms as fragments of other realities — shards of the Feywild, bleeding wounds of the Shadowfell, volcanic eruptions from the Elemental Planes — punch through the silver void and collide with each other in catastrophic convergence events that rewrite the laws of physics across entire regions. On the Material Plane, the effects are already being felt: patches of sky turn silver and translucent, revealing the Astral Sea beyond; gravity reverses in random areas; people dream of places they have never been and wake speaking languages they have never learned. Planar scholars call it the Convergence, and they are terrified.

At the heart of the crisis is the Confluence — not a creature, not a god, but something older: a living equation, a self-aware mathematical principle that existed before the planes were separated. When the multiverse was young and all realities occupied the same space, the Confluence was the organizing intelligence that held everything together. Then the gods carved the multiverse into distinct planes, and the Confluence was shattered — its fragments scattered across the Astral Sea, dormant, forgotten. Now those fragments are waking up. Each one remembers the unity that existed before the planes were split, and each one is pulling its surroundings back toward that primordial state. Left unchecked, the fragments will reassemble, the Confluence will complete itself, and every plane of existence will collapse back into the singular, undifferentiated chaos that preceded creation. Not destruction — something worse. The obliteration of distinction itself. No Material Plane, no Feywild, no Shadowfell, no Heaven, no Hell. Just one infinite, incomprehensible everything that no mortal mind could survive experiencing.

The party enters the Astral Sea through a shattered planar boundary, drawn by visions and portents that mark them as Threadwalkers — mortals whose souls resonate with the boundaries between planes, giving them the ability to navigate convergence zones without being dissolved. They are not the first Threadwalkers. An order of planar monks called the Astral Wardens has guarded the boundaries for millennia, but they are overwhelmed and their monastery — the Threshold Citadel — teeters on the edge of a convergence zone that threatens to swallow it whole. The Wardens' leader, the ancient githzerai Zerith-Ka, believes the only way to stop the Convergence is to find and neutralize each Confluence fragment before they can reassemble. But the fragments are lodged in the most dangerous places in the Astral Sea: the dream-haunted corpse of a dead god, a crucible where three planes have already collided and fused into something new and terrible, and the Spire of Echoes — the place where the Confluence itself is reforming, guarded by entities that believe the reunification of the planes is not a catastrophe but a salvation. The party must decide: is the Confluence an existential threat, or is the separation of the planes the true crime? And if the answer is not as simple as Zerith-Ka believes, what do you do when saving reality means choosing which version of reality to save?
hook: It begins with the dreams. Every night for a week, you dream of the same thing: a vast silver ocean with no horizon, no shore, no surface — just endless luminous void in every direction, and you are floating in it, weightless and breathless and utterly alone. Except you are not alone. Something is out there in the silver. Something enormous and patient and aware. It does not speak, but you understand it the way you understand gravity — a fundamental pull, a direction that your soul leans toward without your permission. On the seventh night, the dream changes. The silver ocean cracks. Fissures of impossible color rip across the void — jade green, arterial red, void-black, sun-gold — and through each crack you glimpse another world: a forest of crystal trees, a city of living shadow, a sea of liquid fire. The worlds are crashing into each other, grinding together like tectonic plates, and the sound they make is not a sound at all but a feeling — the sensation of everything you have ever known being compressed into a single point. You wake up screaming, and the scream keeps going, because the ceiling of your room has turned transparent and through it you can see the Astral Sea — real, vast, and close enough to touch. A figure floats in the silver void above your bed: a githzerai monk in threadbare robes, ancient beyond reckoning, her eyes burning with silver light. She extends a hand and speaks a single sentence that brands itself into your memory: 'The planes are falling into each other. You can feel it. Come.' Then the ceiling seals shut and she is gone. But on your nightstand, where nothing was before, lies a silver compass that points at nothing in this world — its needle spinning, searching, yearning toward something beyond the sky.

setting.name: The Astral Sea and the Convergence Zones
setting.description: The Astral Sea is the connective tissue of the multiverse — a boundless silver void that fills the space between all planes of existence. It has no true geography in the conventional sense: there is no ground, no sky, no weather, no time. Movement is governed by thought — you travel by thinking about your destination, and the speed of your travel is determined by the force of your will (Intelligence score × 3 in feet per round). The silver void is not empty, however. Enormous chunks of solid matter drift through the Astral like islands in a cosmic archipelago: fragments of destroyed demiplanes, the petrified corpses of dead gods (some the size of mountains, their divine features still recognizable), abandoned githyanki fortresses, and stranger things — geometric impossibilities, crystallized memories, frozen moments of time visible as three-dimensional tableaux. Color pools — shimmering discs of chromatic energy — serve as portals to other planes, their colors indicating their destination. And now, the convergence zones: regions where the boundaries between planes have collapsed entirely, creating hybrid realities where the rules of multiple worlds apply simultaneously. A convergence zone might be a forest that is simultaneously on fire and frozen, or a city where gravity pulls in six different directions depending on which plane's physics are dominant in that section. These zones are growing, spreading, consuming more of the Astral Sea with each passing day.
setting.atmosphere: The Astral Sea inspires awe and existential vertigo in equal measure. The silver void stretches in every direction without end, and the absence of ground, horizon, or reference points creates a profound sense of cosmic insignificance. Objects in the distance could be a mile away or a thousand miles — scale is meaningless without landmarks. Sound carries strangely: whispers can be heard across vast distances while shouts are swallowed by the void. The light has no source but suffuses everything with a luminous silver glow that casts no shadows. Time does not pass in the Astral — you do not age, hunger, or tire, though your mind still tracks the passage of events. This creates an eerie dissociation: you feel alert and rested even after what should be days of travel, and the urgency of your mission wars with the Astral's seductive timelessness. Near convergence zones, the atmosphere shifts dramatically: the silver void fractures into competing realities, each bleeding its own colors, sounds, and sensations into the space around it. The air might taste of ash and roses simultaneously. Gravity might pull you toward a floating continent of shadow-stuff while a wind from the Elemental Plane of Air tries to fling you into a color pool leading to the Feywild. The deeper into the Convergence you go, the more reality itself becomes negotiable — and the harder it becomes to remember which version of physics you're supposed to be obeying.

regions.name: The Silver Wastes
regions.description: The outermost region of the Astral Sea accessible from the Material Plane — a vast expanse of silver void dotted with drifting debris, ancient ruins, and the first signs of convergence damage. The Threshold Citadel, monastery of the Astral Wardens, anchors this region: a fortress of crystal and thought-stone that has guarded the planar boundaries for ten thousand years. But the citadel is cracking. Convergence stress fractures run through its walls, and entire wings have been swallowed by encroaching zones where Astral silver bleeds into Shadowfell darkness. Githyanki raiding parties prowl the wastes, drawn by the chaos, and psychic predators — astral dreadnoughts, thought-eaters, and things without names — circle the weakening boundaries like sharks around a wounded whale. The Silver Wastes are the party's staging ground, the place where they learn to navigate the Astral and understand the scope of the crisis before venturing deeper.

regions.name: The Dead God's Cradle
regions.description: Deep in the Astral Sea, the petrified corpse of Auldrath, a forgotten god of boundaries and thresholds, tumbles slowly through the void. Auldrath died during the Dawn War — or was murdered, depending on which surviving texts you trust — and its body has drifted here for millennia, slowly calcifying into a continent-sized mass of divine stone. But Auldrath was the god of boundaries, and its death did not destroy its portfolio — it merely made it unmanaged. Now, with the Convergence awakening, Auldrath's corpse has become a beacon. A Confluence fragment is lodged in the dead god's skull like a tumor, pulsing with the memory of a unified multiverse, and the divine essence still saturating the corpse is amplifying the fragment's power a thousandfold. The corpse itself is a dungeon of cosmic proportions: vast caverns carved from divine bone, chambers filled with crystallized memories of the god's life, parasitic ecosystems of creatures that feed on residual divinity, and the persistent, maddening sensation that something in the corpse is still dreaming.

regions.name: The Planar Crucible
regions.description: Where three planes have already collided and fused into something unprecedented: a region where the Feywild, the Shadowfell, and the Elemental Plane of Fire occupy the same space simultaneously. The result is a landscape of impossible contradictions — forests of shadow-trees that burn with fey fire without being consumed, rivers of liquid darkness that steam where they meet volcanic glass, meadows of ash-flowers that bloom and die and bloom again in endless cycles. The Crucible is not stable; it pulses and shifts as the three merged planes compete for dominance, and pockets of pure single-plane reality create dangerous transition zones where the laws of physics change without warning. A Confluence fragment sits at the Crucible's heart, holding the three planes together like a keystone in an arch. Removing it might separate the planes — or it might cause the entire region to explode into planar shrapnel. The inhabitants of the Crucible have adapted to their hybrid existence and do not want to be 'fixed.' Fire genasi shamans, shadow fey aristocrats, and eladrin druids have formed an unlikely society in the merged space, and they will fight to protect their impossible home.

regions.name: The Spire of Echoes
regions.description: At the heart of the Convergence, where the density of planar collisions reaches critical mass, the Spire of Echoes rises from the chaos like a needle through fabric. It is not a building in any conventional sense — it is a structure made of crystallized planar boundaries, translucent walls showing glimpses of every plane of existence simultaneously. The Spire is where the Confluence is reassembling itself, each recovered fragment adding to a growing intelligence that remembers what the multiverse was before the gods divided it. The entity that speaks from the Spire's apex does not threaten or demand — it explains, calmly and persuasively, that the separation of the planes was the original violence, that the Convergence is a healing, and that resistance is not evil but simply misguided. The final confrontation is not a battle against a monster but a philosophical crisis given physical form: do you preserve the multiverse as it is, flawed and divided, or do you allow it to return to a unity that might be perfect but would erase everything that individuality and separation have created? The Spire is guarded by Echoes — reflections of the party themselves from alternate timelines where they made different choices — and by Convergence Heralds, beings from the merged realities who see the reunification as paradise.

explorationRules: The Astral Sea requires a fundamentally different approach to navigation than terrestrial travel. Movement is thought-based: a character's travel speed is determined by Intelligence score × 3 feet per round in combat, or roughly 10 miles per hour of subjective travel for exploration. Characters with low Intelligence can be towed by allies. The party does not need food, water, or sleep in the Astral Sea — time does not pass for their bodies — but their minds still experience the passage of events, and prolonged exposure to the Astral's timelessness requires DC 12 Wisdom saves every subjective 'day' to avoid existential disorientation (disadvantage on Wisdom checks for 1d4 hours on failure). Navigation between regions requires a DC 14 Intelligence (Arcana) check using the silver compass or similar planar navigation tool; failure results in a detour through a random encounter zone. Each subjective day of travel, the DM rolls 1d6: on a 1-2, the party encounters drifting debris with potential salvage or hazards; on a 3, they encounter a convergence micro-zone (a small area where two planes overlap); on a 4, they encounter astral denizens (githyanki patrols, astral dreadnoughts at a distance, psychic predators, or friendly travelers); on a 5-6, travel is uneventful. Convergence zones are marked by chromatic distortion visible from great distances — the silver void fractures into competing colors that indicate which planes are colliding. Entering a convergence zone requires a DC 15 Wisdom save or the character suffers planar dissonance (confused for 1 round as contradictory physics assault their senses). Threadwalkers (the party) make this save with advantage. Color pools — portals to other planes — dot the Astral Sea and can be identified by color: silver leads to the Material Plane, emerald to the Feywild, onyx to the Shadowfell, crimson to the Plane of Fire, and so on. Misidentifying a color pool (DC 13 Arcana to read correctly) can strand the party on the wrong plane. The silver compass given by Zerith-Ka always points toward the nearest Confluence fragment, growing warmer as the party approaches.
